The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Language Embeddings Sometimes Contain Typological Generalizations
papers.research_question: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? Which typological features can be discovered when the system is not told what to look for?
papers.core_contribution: This paper finds that neural models can sometimes learn typological generalizations in their language representations, but less readily than suggested by prior work, and that careful evaluation is essential to avoid false positives. It also releases several resources for 1295 languages.
papers.conclusion: Neural models can discover typological generalizations, but they do so less readily than suggested by previous research, and careful evaluation is necessary to confirm such discoveries.
papers.key_findings:
Some generalizations in learned language representations are surprisingly close to traditional typological features, but most models (including those from previous work) do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations.
Careful attention to evaluation details, such as controlling for genealogical and areal correlations, is essential to avoid false positives.
The word-level language model (WordLM) captures word order features and some morphological features, while many other models (including MTVec, MTCell, and Ö&T) show little evidence of encoding typological features when evaluated with their method.
Lexical baselines (ASJP and Lexical similarity vectors) do not encode structural features, as expected, and can serve as a baseline for evaluation.
papers.limitation: The study only tries to connect neural language representations with known features from the typological literature, not with potentially novel generalizations.
future_direction: Investigating whether models make typological generalizations that human linguists have not previously made.
papers.abstract: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? We explore these questions by training neural models for a range of natural language processing tasks on a massively multilingual dataset of Bible translations in 1295 languages. The learned language representations are then compared to existing typological databases as well as to a novel set of quantitative syntactic and morphological features obtained through annotation projection. We conclude that some generalizations are surprisingly close to traditional features from linguistic typology, but that most of our models, as well as those of previous work, do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations. Careful attention to details in the evaluation turns out to be essential to avoid false positives. Furthermore, to encourage continued work in this field, we release several resources covering most or all of the languages in our data: (i) multiple sets of language representations, (ii) multilingual word embeddings, (iii) projected and predicted syntactic and morphological features, (iv) software to provide linguistically sound evaluations of language representations.

papers.title: Model-Aware Tokenizer Transfer
papers.research_question: How can we effectively adapt a pretrained large language model to a new language by transferring its tokenizer, using model internals (attention patterns) rather than just semantic heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model-Aware Tokenizer Transfer (MATT), a method that uses an Attention Influence Modeling (AIM) objective to distill inter-token communication patterns from a source model into a target model with a new tokenizer, providing an efficient warm-up before language modeling and outperforming heuristic baselines.
papers.conclusion: MATT is an effective and efficient model-aware method for tokenizer transfer that leverages attention dynamics to bridge the performance gap caused by tokenizer changes, offering a practical path for multilingual LLM adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
MATT recovers a large fraction of the original model's performance on discriminative and generative tasks within a few GPU hours.
MATT consistently outperforms heuristic-based tokenizer transfer methods like WECHSEL, FOCUS, and Transtokenizers across multiple languages and model scales.
The AIM objective provides a rich learning signal, allowing more than 50% of final performance gains to be achieved in under 10% of total training steps.
MATT is most effective when input and output embeddings are tied, but still offers advantages even when they are not.
Applying AIM to higher layers improves performance but saturates at around one-third of the model's depth, with computational cost growing linearly.
papers.limitation:
MATT relies on tied input and output embeddings to fully realize its advantages.
The method has not been tested on encoder-only architectures.
The evaluation does not include continual pretraining due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing strategies to handle untied input and output embeddings.
Testing MATT on encoder-only architectures by removing the causal constraint in AIM.
Exploring adaptive data selection to prioritize documents with unseen tokens for faster training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained to support an increasing number of languages, yet their predefined tokenizers remain a bottleneck for adapting models to lower-resource or distinct-script languages. Existing tokenizer transfer methods typically rely on semantic heuristics to initialize new embeddings, ignoring higher-layer model dynamics and limiting transfer quality. We propose Model-Aware Tokenizer Transfer (MATT), a method that incorporates model internals into the tokenizer transfer process. MATT introduces an Attention Influence Modeling (AIM) objective that distills inter-token communication patterns from a source model into a target model with a new tokenizer, providing an efficient warm-up before standard language modeling. Unlike approaches that focus solely on embedding similarity, MATT leverages attention behavior to guide embedding initialization and adaptation. Experiments across diverse linguistic settings show that MATT recovers a large fraction of the original model's performance within a few GPU hours, outperforming heuristic baselines. These results demonstrate that incorporating model-level signals offers a practical and effective path toward robust tokenizer transfer in multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Transformer Attention for Multilingual Translation
papers.research_question: How do multilingual Transformer models pay attention when translating different language pairs? We analyze the functions and behaviors of attention heads in self-attention and cross-attention.
papers.core_contribution: Different language pairs tend to share the same attention heads for functions like syntax and reordering, but language interference reduces head accuracies. Additionally, deep-layer cross-attention heads cooperate to learn multiple reordering options due to multiple valid translations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual Transformer models share attention heads for similar functions across languages, but language interference reduces head accuracies. Deep-layer cross-attention heads cooperate to handle multiple valid reorderings in translation.
papers.key_findings:
Different language pairs share the same attention heads for functions such as syntax and reordering.
Language interference in multilingual models reduces the accuracy of function heads compared to bilingual models.
Deep-layer cross-attention heads work cooperatively to learn different options for word reordering, likely because there are multiple valid translations for a source sentence.
The Transformer decoder uses shallow-layer cross-attention heads for current word alignment and deep-layer heads for next word alignment.
Automatic pruning can remove a large fraction of attention heads without significant loss in translation quality.
papers.limitation: The study covers only six translation directions with limited typological diversity, due to the need for ground truth word alignments.
future_direction: Investigate multilingual models covering many more languages with more linguistic diversity following the same methodology.
papers.abstract: Transformers are the predominant model for machine translation. Recent works also showed that a single Transformer model can be trained to learn translation for multiple different language pairs, achieving promising results. In this work, we investigate how the multilingual Transformer model pays attention for translating different language pairs. We first performed automatic pruning to eliminate a large number of noisy heads and then analyzed the functions and behaviors of the remaining heads in both self-attention and cross-attention. We find that different language pairs, in spite of having different syntax and word orders, tended to share the same heads for the same functions, such as syntax heads and reordering heads. However, the different characteristics of different language pairs clearly caused interference in function heads and affected head accuracies. Additionally, we reveal an interesting behavior of the Transformer cross-attention: the deep-layer cross-attention heads work in a clear cooperative way to learn different options for word reordering, which can be caused by the nature of translation tasks having multiple different gold translations in the target language for the same source sentence.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Feature Aggregation in Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer Using Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: Do the lower layers of mBERT provide complementary information to the last layer for zero-shot cross-lingual downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Lower layers of mBERT provide complementary information to the last layer for zero-shot cross-lingual tasks, and a feature aggregation module (DLFA) is proposed to fuse this information, improving performance.
papers.conclusion: Different layers of mBERT contain diverse cross-lingual and language structure information, and the proposed DLFA module effectively integrates this information to improve zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance.
papers.key_findings:
Aggregating lower layers with the last layer improves performance on XNLI, PAWS-X, NER, and POS tasks.
Lower layers of mBERT are more important for cross-lingual transfer, while upper layers are more important for language structure.
The proposed DLFA module effectively fuses global and local information from two layers.
The method generalizes to other models like XLM-R-base.
Different tasks benefit from fusing different layers (e.g., layer 8 for NER, layer 10 for POS).
future_direction: Pay more attention to the rich information contained in different layers of mBERT and apply them to more downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Multilingual BERT (mBERT), a language model pre-trained on large multilingual corpora, has impressive zero-shot cross-lingual transfer capabilities and performs surprisingly well on zero-shot POS tagging and Named Entity Recognition (NER), as well as on cross-lingual model transfer. At present, the mainstream methods to solve the cross-lingual downstream tasks are always using the last transformer layer's output of mBERT as the representation of linguistic information. In this work, we explore the complementary property of lower layers to the last transformer layer of mBERT. A feature aggregation module based on an attention mechanism is proposed to fuse the information contained in different layers of mBERT. The experiments are conducted on four zero-shot cross-lingual transfer datasets, and the proposed method obtains performance improvements on key multilingual benchmark tasks XNLI (+1.5 %), PAWS-X (+2.4 %), NER (+1.2 F1), and POS (+1.5 F1). Through the analysis of the experimental results, we prove that the layers before the last layer of mBERT can provide extra useful information for cross-lingual downstream tasks and explore the interpretability of mBERT empirically.

papers.title: When Meanings Meet: Investigating the Emergence and Quality of Shared Concept Spaces during Multilingual Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How do shared, language-agnostic concept spaces emerge and develop during the multilingual pretraining of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Shared concept spaces emerge early in multilingual pretraining and remain relatively stable, but alignment with these spaces is language-dependent and influenced by training data composition.
papers.conclusion: Shared concept spaces emerge early and are progressively refined during multilingual pretraining, with alignment depending on language and data composition. Targeted multi-aligned data can improve alignment for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Shared concept spaces arise early in pretraining and continue to refine throughout training.
Alignment with shared concept spaces depends on language similarity and training data proportion.
Cross-lingual concept patching can shift model behavior, such as selecting dominant senses for polysemous words or translating cross-lingual homographs instead of copying them.
The model initially prefers copying input words over translating them, a behavior learned early.
Patching from averaged representations across languages (the 'seen' setting) is often as effective as patching from English-only representations for inducing concepts in English output.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on a single, relatively small model (EuroLLM-1.7B), though provides supporting evidence on two others.
Analysis is restricted to nouns; behavior of other word classes is not studied.
Inherits biases from the Multi-SimLex dataset, such as ambiguous translations for polysemous words.
Focuses only on the simple task of word-level translation; findings may not generalize to more complex tasks.
future_direction: Investigate how representations for other word classes (beyond nouns) behave.
Study the emergence and behavior of language-agnostic spaces for more complex multilingual tasks like sentence-level translation or reasoning.
papers.abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) with high multilingual coverage is becoming increasingly important -- especially when monolingual resources are scarce. Recent studies have found that LLMs process multilingual inputs in shared concept spaces, thought to support generalization and cross-lingual transfer. However, these prior studies often do not use causal methods, lack deeper error analysis or focus on the final model only, leaving open how these spaces emerge during training. We investigate the development of language-agnostic concept spaces during pretraining of EuroLLM through the causal interpretability method of activation patching. We isolate cross-lingual concept representations, then inject them into a translation prompt to investigate how consistently translations can be altered, independently of the language. We find that shared concept spaces emerge early} and continue to refine, but that alignment with them is language-dependent}. Furthermore, in contrast to prior work, our fine-grained manual analysis reveals that some apparent gains in translation quality reflect shifts in behavior -- like selecting senses for polysemous words or translating instead of copying cross-lingual homographs -- rather than improved translation ability. Our findings offer new insight into the training dynamics of cross-lingual alignment and the conditions under which causal interpretability methods offer meaningful insights in multilingual contexts.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Language Models Remember Facts?
papers.research_question: How do factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs, and when does language play a role in recall?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall mechanisms in multilingual LLMs share similarities with English LLMs but with key differences, such as the role of MLPs in extraction and the composition of relation and language in the last token's function vector.
papers.conclusion: These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies—such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition—that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture.
Subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent.
The last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted.
In decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose relation and language in two separate stages.
MLPs play a more prominent role in extraction in multilingual LLMs compared to English LLMs.
papers.limitation: Excluded languages with too few examples, limiting the analysis to a subset of languages.
future_direction: Developing new methodologies for knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition tailored for multilingual LLMs
Studying whether models 'think' in English by examining how the function vector is altered across languages
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) store and retrieve vast amounts of factual knowledge acquired during pre-training. Prior research has localized and identified mechanisms behind knowledge recall; however, it has only focused on English monolingual models. The question of how these mechanisms generalize to non-English languages and multilingual LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of three multilingual LLMs. First, we show that previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture. Next, through patching intermediate representations, we localize the role of language during recall, finding that subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent. Additionally, we discover that the last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted from the subject. Furthermore, in decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose these two pieces of information in two separate stages. These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies -- such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition -- that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Exploring Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation: Mutual Opportunities and Open Challenges
papers.research_question: Can LLMs leverage both their robust capabilities (in English) and their multilingual knowledge (in non-English languages) during inference to further unlock their multilingual potential?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation (X Transplant), a probing framework that transplants latent activations across languages at inference time to unlock multilingual and cultural knowledge in LLMs, revealing underutilized potential.
papers.conclusion: The analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
X Transplant has mutually beneficial effects on multilingual capability and cultural adaptability, especially for low-resource languages and cultures.
Attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge.
The upper-bound performance of X Transplant reveals a significant underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential.
English boosts multilingual capability, while non-English improves cultural adaptability.
papers.abstract: Current large language models (LLMs) often exhibit imbalances in multilingual capabilities and cultural adaptability, largely attributed to their English-centric pre-training data. In this paper, we introduce and investigate a cross-lingual latent transplantation (XTransplant) framework, which aims to further exploit the model's internalized multilingual knowledge during inference and examine its effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs. XTransplant framework enables models to harness the complementary strengths of both English and non-English resources by transplanting latent activations across languages. Through extensive analysis, we empirically demonstrate that XTransplant, a form of cross-lingual interaction, has mutually beneficial effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs, particularly for low-resource languages and cultures. We further reveal that attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge. In addition, we conduct in-depth analysis of XTransplant's stability, effectiveness, and generalizability. By probing the upper bound performance of XTransplant, we expose the considerable underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential-a challenge that remains open. We hope our analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.

papers.title: Layer Swapping for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we facilitate cross-lingual transfer of mathematical reasoning capabilities to non-English languages without in-language math data by merging models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces layer swapping, a model merging method that swaps top and bottom transformer layers from a language expert into a math expert to enable zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of mathematical reasoning without in-language task data.
papers.conclusion: Layer swapping is an effective, flexible, and inexpensive method for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of reasoning capabilities, with potential for broader application in multilingual LLM development.
papers.key_findings:
Layer swapping outperforms individual experts and model souping on the MGSM benchmark by an average of 10% across four languages (Swahili, Telugu, Bengali, Japanese).
Analysis of fine-tuning updates shows math capabilities are concentrated in middle transformer layers, while language capabilities are in the top and bottom layers.
The method is simple, inexpensive, and fully post hoc, requiring no further training or in-language task data.
The method provides the biggest benefit for lower-resource languages where cross-lingual transfer during standard fine-tuning is limited.
Transition zones between swapped layers were not necessary in the tested setting but are included as a component of the methodology.
papers.limitation:
The method was only evaluated on one model size (LLAMA 3.1 8B) and a limited set of languages and tasks (mathematical reasoning).
The experts were not fine-tuned for very long, which may affect the need for transition zones and the generalizability of the findings.
future_direction: Testing the method with frozen parameters from the start of training.
Applying layer swapping to LLMs with different pretraining distributions (e.g., balanced multilingual pretraining).
Extending the method to other reasoning tasks, parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings, and different training stages.
papers.abstract: Model merging, such as model souping, is the practice of combining different models with the same architecture together without further training. In this work, we present a model merging methodology that addresses the difficulty of fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) for target tasks in non-English languages, where task-specific data is often unavailable. We focus on mathematical reasoning and without in-language math data, facilitate cross-lingual transfer by composing language and math capabilities. Starting from the same pretrained model, we fine-tune separate "experts" on math instruction data in English and on generic instruction data in the target language. We then replace the top and bottom transformer layers of the math expert directly with layers from the language expert, which consequently enhances math performance in the target language. The resulting merged models outperform the individual experts and other merging methods on the math benchmark, MGSM, by 10% across four major languages where math instruction data is scarce. In addition, this layer swapping is simple, inexpensive, and intuitive, as it is based on an interpretative analysis of the most important parameter changes during the fine-tuning of each expert. The ability to successfully re-compose LLMs for cross-lingual transfer in this manner opens up future possibilities to combine model expertise, create modular solutions, and transfer reasoning capabilities across languages all post hoc.

papers.title: Locating Language-Specific Information in Contextualized Embeddings
papers.research_question: How is language-specific information stored in multilingual pretrained language model representations, and can it be located in linear subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: This paper locates language-specific information in multilingual pretrained language models by projecting representations into linear subspaces using DensRay and LDA, showing that such information is scattered across dimensions and more prevalent in lower layers.
papers.conclusion: Language-specific information in multilingual representations can be decoded via linear subspaces, with dimensionality varying by task and lower layers being more language-specific, offering insights for improving cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific information is scattered across many dimensions and can be projected into a linear subspace.
The dimensionality of the language-specific subspace is task-dependent, with an upper bound roughly equal to the number of languages.
Lower layers of the models store more language-specific information compared to higher layers.
The proposed activity regularization method L-DAR can slightly improve zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance in some cases.
For the NER task with multisource training, L-DAR does not consistently improve performance, indicating limitations.
papers.limitation: The activity regularization approach L-DAR leads to a performance drop on the NER task with multisource training, which is not fully understood and left for future research.
future_direction: Continuing research to better utilize language-specific information for improved zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models (MPLMs) exhibit multilinguality and are well suited for transfer across languages. Most MPLMs are trained in an unsupervised fashion and the relationship between their objective and multilinguality is unclear. More specifically, the question whether MPLM representations are language-agnostic or they simply interleave well with learned task prediction heads arises. In this work, we locate language-specific information in MPLMs and identify its dimensionality and the layers where this information occurs. We show that language-specific information is scattered across many dimensions, which can be projected into a linear subspace. Our study contributes to a better understanding of MPLM representations, going beyond treating them as unanalyzable blobs of information.

papers.title: What Language(s) Does Aya-23 Think In? How Multilinguality Affects Internal Language Representations
papers.research_question: How does balanced multilingual training affect internal language processing in LLMs, specifically in terms of language activation, neuron sharing, and layer-wise distribution of language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Balanced multilingual training leads to distinct internal language processing, with language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of typologically related languages during translation, unlike English-centric models.
papers.conclusion: Balanced multilingual training fundamentally alters how decoder-only LLMs process language internally, leading to language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of multiple languages during translation.
papers.key_findings:
Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language.
Code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one.
Aya-23’s language-specific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models.
Neuron overlap analysis shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types.
French-based code-mixed inputs show higher neuron clustering than Chinese-based inputs across all models, regardless of training data composition.
papers.limitation:
Token overlap between languages in the logit lens experiments may affect analysis of language-specific activation patterns.
Neuron specialization analysis using binary activations results in information loss that may obscure subtle activation patterns.
Code-mixed dataset created via rule-based word-to-word translation produces unnatural sentences that may not represent authentic code-switching.
Analysis is limited to three models and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multilingual tasks, yet their internal language processing remains poorly understood. We analyze how Aya-23-8B, a decoder-only LLM trained on balanced multilingual data, handles code-mixed, cloze, and translation tasks compared to predominantly monolingual models like Llama 3 and Chinese-LLaMA-2. Using logit lens and neuron specialization analyses, we find: (1) Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language; (2) code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one; and (3) Aya-23's languagespecific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models. Neuron overlap analysis further shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types. These findings reveal how multilingual training shapes LLM internals and inform future cross-lingual transfer research.

papers.title: Language Lives in Sparse Dimensions: Toward Interpretable and Efficient Multilingual Control for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode language identity, and can we identify sparse, consistent dimensions that control the cross-lingual transition from shared representations to language-specific token spaces?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that cross-lingual transfer in LLMs is governed by a sparse, consistent set of language-specific dimensions in the residual stream, and introduces a training-free method to identify and manipulate these dimensions for controlled language switching.
papers.conclusion: Language-specific dimensions are a consistent and controllable mechanism underlying cross-lingual transfer in LLMs, enabling efficient and interpretable multilingual control through simple, training-free interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific dimensions are sparse and appear at consistent indices across intermediate to final layers of LLMs.
These dimensions can be identified with as few as 50 sentences of parallel or monolingual data.
Intervening on these dimensions by overwriting their values can switch the model's output language while preserving semantic content.
The proposed method outperforms prior neuron-based approaches (Neuron-Kojima and Neuron-Tang) on a multilingual generation control task.
There is significant overlap in language-specific dimensions across typologically similar languages (e.g., Chinese and Japanese share many dimensions).
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters (e.g., anchor layer, scaling coefficient) were primarily tuned on Llama2-7B and transferred to other models (Llama3.1-8B, Aya23-8B), which may be suboptimal.
Evaluation is limited to multilingual generation control and question answering tasks; broader impact on downstream tasks (e.g., mathematics, summarization) and robustness across prompt formulations remains unexamined.
future_direction: Conduct systematic per-model hyperparameter search to optimize performance for each model individually.
Extend evaluation to a broader range of downstream tasks, incorporate task-specific metrics and human judgments, and assess robustness across different prompt formulations.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities despite limited exposure to non-English data. Prior studies show that English-centric large language models map multilingual content into English-aligned representations at intermediate layers and then project them back into target-language token spaces in the final layer. From this observation, we hypothesize that this cross-lingual transition is governed by a small and sparse set of dimensions, which occur at consistent indices across the intermediate to final layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a simple, training-free method to identify and manipulate these dimensions, requiring only as few as 50 sentences of either parallel or monolingual data. Experiments on a multilingual generation control task reveal the interpretability of these dimensions, demonstrating that the interventions in these dimensions can switch the output language while preserving semantic content, and that it surpasses the performance of prior neuron-based approaches at a substantially lower cost.

papers.title: A multilabel approach to morphosyntactic probing
papers.research_question: How well does multilingual BERT encode morphosyntactic features across languages, and which features are recognized as shared cross-linguistically?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a multilabel probing paradigm for morphosyntactic analysis and demonstrates that multilingual BERT encodes many morphosyntactic features extractably, with some features shared cross-linguistically.
papers.conclusion: Multilabel probing is an effective method for analyzing morphosyntactic representations in multilingual language models, revealing that mBERT encodes many features and that some are represented cross-linguistically.
papers.key_findings:
mBERT-6 holds the most morphosyntactic information, with probes achieving micro-averaged F1 scores between 0.83 and 0.97 for seven languages.
Multilingual probes slightly underperform monolingual probes but exhibit better selectivity, suggesting less memorization.
Cross-lingual transfer experiments show that nouns and verbs are well transferred, while adjectives and nominative case are less consistently recognized across languages.
The multilabel paradigm enables fine-grained analysis of feature co-occurrence and agreement patterns, as demonstrated in a case study of Hebrew determiners.
Probe performance varies across languages due to differences in feature sets and training set sizes, making direct comparison difficult.
papers.limitation: The UD corpora used are from narrow domains (e.g., Wikipedia, news, Bible) and may not capture the full range of linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Probe different multilingual language models to compare their morphosyntactic representations.
Explore how global and feature-level probe performance corresponds to downstream task performance.
Conduct more detailed analyses of specific features and their cross-linguistic transfer.
papers.abstract: We propose using a multilabel probing task to assess the morphosyntactic representations of multilingual word embeddings. This tweak on canonical probing makes it easy to explore morphosyntactic representations, both holistically and at the level of individual features (e.g., gender, number, case), and leads more naturally to the study of how language models handle co-occurring features (e.g., agreement phenomena). We demonstrate this task with multilingual BERT Through this simple but robust paradigm, we verify that multilingual BERT renders many morphosyntactic features simultaneously extractable. We further evaluate the probes on six held-out languages: Arabic, Chinese, Marathi, Slovenian, Tagalog, and Yorb. This zero-shot style of probing has the added benefit of revealing which cross-linguistic properties a language model recognizes as being shared by multiple languages.

papers.title: Structured World Representations in Maze-Solving Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn to solve mazes and what internal representations do they form?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks learn linear representations of maze connectivity in their residual stream, and specific attention heads (adjacency heads) handle path-following by attending to valid neighbors.
papers.conclusion: Transformers acquire emergent linear representations of maze connectivity encoded in a single token's latent state, and their embedding layers learn spatial structure; specific attention heads are identified that respect maze topology.
papers.key_findings:
The residual stream of a single token (e.g., <PATH_START>) can be linearly decoded to reconstruct the entire maze structure.
The embedding layer learns an emergent spatial structure where distances between coordinate tokens correlate with Manhattan distances on the grid.
Specific attention heads (e.g., Layer 5, Head 3) consistently attend to tokens at path length 1 from the current position, acting as adjacency heads that respect maze topology.
The formation of linearly decodable maze representations coincides with grokking-like transitions where generalization performance improves sharply.
Models often violate maze constraints (e.g., pass through walls) but still reach the target, indicating imperfect learning of constraints.
papers.limitation:
The generalizability of findings from toy models to larger scales remains uncertain.
Models often violate maze constraints (e.g., pass through walls) even when reaching the target.
future_direction: Construct a more complete mechanistic picture of how elementary heads operate over the linear world model to form circuits for solving mazes.
Investigate the generality of emergent models by training different neural network architectures on the same tasks with different input representations.
papers.abstract: Transformer models underpin many recent advances in practical machine learning applications, yet understanding their internal behavior continues to elude researchers. Given the size and complexity of these models, forming a comprehensive picture of their inner workings remains a significant challenge. To this end, we set out to understand small transformer models in a more tractable setting: that of solving mazes. In this work, we focus on the abstractions formed by these models and find evidence for the consistent emergence of structured internal representations of maze topology and valid paths. We demonstrate this by showing that the residual stream of only a single token can be linearly decoded to faithfully reconstruct the entire maze. We also find that the learned embeddings of individual tokens have spatial structure. Furthermore, we take steps towards deciphering the circuity of path-following by identifying attention heads (dubbed $\textit{adjacency heads}$), which are implicated in finding valid subsequent tokens.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Towards a Deep Understanding of Multilingual End-to-End Speech Translation
papers.research_question: Does multilingual end-to-end speech translation exhibit properties similar to multilingual neural machine translation? How are learned representations distributed across languages and layers? Can the model predict linguistic typology features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes multilingual end-to-end speech translation using SVCCA, finding that data quantity is more crucial than linguistic similarity for low-resource languages, and that encoder representations are effective for predicting phonetic typology features.
papers.conclusion: The amount of available data plays a significant role in limiting knowledge transfer across languages in multilingual speech translation. The model's encoder representations perform better on phonetic-related typology features compared to syntax features.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity loses its efficacy in multilingual speech translation when the training data for a specific language is limited.
Enhanced encoder representations and well-aligned audio-text data significantly improve translation quality, surpassing bilingual counterparts when training data is sufficient.
The encoder representations of multilingual speech translation demonstrate superior performance in predicting phonetic features in linguistic typology prediction.
Low-resource languages do not benefit from high-resource languages due to the lack of sufficient data to form language-specific sub-spaces.
Languages from the same language branch tend to cluster together in the representation space as layers deepen.
papers.limitation:
The quality of the LASER-based evaluation datasets may be compromised due to a lower threshold for semantic equivalence, potentially affecting SVCCA analysis reliability.
The analysis lacks a phonological perspective due to the absence of a reliable standard mapping between audio and phoneme, especially for low-resource languages.
future_direction: Addressing data scarcity in the multilingual setting to improve translation quality.
Improving the representation space for individual languages, especially for low-resource languages.
Learning high-quality representation spaces for low-resource languages with limited data to achieve linguistic fairness.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we employ Singular Value Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA) to analyze representations learnt in a multilingual end-to-end speech translation model trained over 22 languages. SVCCA enables us to estimate representational similarity across languages and layers, enhancing our understanding of the functionality of multilingual speech translation and its potential connection to multilingual neural machine translation. The multilingual speech translation model is trained on the CoVoST 2 dataset in all possible directions, and we utilize LASER to extract parallel bitext data for SVCCA analysis. We derive three major findings from our analysis: (I) Linguistic similarity loses its efficacy in multilingual speech translation when the training data for a specific language is limited. (II) Enhanced encoder representations and well-aligned audio-text data significantly improve translation quality, surpassing the bilingual counterparts when the training data is not compromised. (III) The encoder representations of multilingual speech translation demonstrate superior performance in predicting phonetic features in linguistic typology prediction. With these findings, we propose that releasing the constraint of limited data for low-resource languages and subsequently combining them with linguistically related high-resource languages could offer a more effective approach for multilingual end-to-end speech translation.

papers.title: Counterfactually Probing Language Identity in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: How is language identity encoded and used in multilingual language models, and can it be causally manipulated to affect the language of generated tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Language identity is linearly encoded in multilingual models and can be causally manipulated via counterfactual probing to systematically increase the probability of words from a target language in masked language modeling, but not specifically towards translation-equivalent words.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual models like mBERT and XLM-R have both language-specific and language-general components, and counterfactual probing (AlterRep) can be fruitfully applied to manipulate language identity in these models.
papers.key_findings:
Pushing token embeddings towards a target language (e.g., Spanish) in a template of another language (e.g., English) increases the probability of words from the target language and decreases the probability of words from the template language.
Pushing embeddings in the same direction as the template language does not significantly increase the probability of the target word but makes the model more likely to generate words from that language overall.
The manipulation leaves words from a third control language largely unaffected, indicating specificity.
The results hold for both monolingual and code-mixed training data, and for language pairs with different scripts and families.
The findings provide evidence that multilingual models contain both language-specific and language-general components.
papers.limitation:
Techniques like INLP extract only linearly extractable information; more complex non-linear methods might be needed for other properties.
The method is sensitive to parameters like α and the number of INLP iterations, and choosing them is non-trivial.
The results do not demonstrate practical utility for tasks like machine translation.
future_direction: Exploring the use of more complex, non-linear methods (like those proposed by Ravfogel et al., 2022) for manipulating model representations.
Applying the method to explore linguistic typology in multilingual model space.
Translating the results into practical applications.
papers.abstract: Techniques in causal analysis of language models illuminate how linguistic information is organized in LLMs.We use one such technique, AlterRep, a method of counterfactual probing, to explore the internal structure of multilingual models (mBERT and XLM-R).We train a linear classifier on a binary language identity task, to classify tokens between Language X and Language Y. Applying a counterfactual probing procedure, we use the classifier weights to project the embeddings into the null space and push the resulting embeddings either in the direction of Language X or Language Y. Then we evaluate on a masked language modeling task.We find that, given a template in Language X, pushing towards Language Y systematically increases the probability of Language Y words, above and beyond a third-party control language.But it does not specifically push the model towards translation-equivalent words in Language Y. Pushing towards Language X (the same direction as the template) has a minimal effect, but somewhat degrades these models.Overall, we take these results as further evidence of the rich structure of massive multilingual language models, which include both a language-specific and language-general component.And we show that counterfactual probing can be fruitfully applied to multilingual models.

papers.title: AlignX: Advancing Multilingual Large Language Models with Multilingual Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: How to improve multilingual performance and cross-lingual alignment in large language models for non-dominant languages?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes AlignX, a two-stage representation-level framework that aligns multilingual representations in LLMs through contrastive learning and language matching, improving multilingual general and cross-lingual generation capabilities.
papers.conclusion: AlignX effectively enhances multilingual general and cross-lingual generation capabilities by aligning multilingual representations, as demonstrated on multiple LLMs and benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
AlignX improves multilingual general capability across multiple benchmarks and base LLMs.
AlignX enhances cross-lingual generation capability, achieving higher BLEU scores on FLORES-101.
Scaling AlignX to 51 languages further improves performance without the curse of multilinguality.
The instruction contrastive learning facilitates knowledge sharing, and language matching promotes accurate cross-lingual generation.
AlignX brings multilingual representations closer in the intermediate layers.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) possess impressive multilingual understanding and generation capabilities. However, their performance and cross-lingual alignment often lag for non-dominant languages. A common solution is to fine-tune LLMs on large-scale and more balanced multilingual corpus, but such approaches often lead to imprecise alignment and suboptimal knowledge transfer, struggling with limited improvements across languages. In this paper, we propose AlignX to bridge the multilingual performance gap, which is a two-stage representation-level framework for enhancing multilingual performance of pre-trained LLMs. In the first stage, we align multilingual representations with multilingual semantic alignment and language feature integration. In the second stage, we stimulate the multilingual capability of LLMs via multilingual instruction fine-tuning. Experimental results on several pre-trained LLMs demonstrate that our approach enhances LLMs' multilingual general and cross-lingual generation capability. Further analysis indicates that AlignX brings the multilingual representations closer and improves the cross-lingual alignment.

papers.title: Tracing Multilingual Factual Knowledge Acquisition in Pretraining
papers.research_question: How do factual recall and crosslingual consistency evolve during pretraining in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This work traces the development of multilingual factual recall and crosslingual consistency during pretraining, identifying two primary pathways: frequency-driven learning (dominant and language-agnostic) and crosslingual transfer (limited and constrained to certain relation types).
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that multilingual factual knowledge acquisition in LLMs is driven by two distinct pathways: frequency-driven learning and crosslingual transfer, with the former being dominant and the latter limited in scale and scope.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual factual recall develops progressively during pretraining, with English and distant languages converging early, while similar-script languages improve with extended training.
Fact frequency in the pretraining corpus is a strong predictor of factual recall accuracy across languages, with high-frequency facts more likely to be recalled correctly.
Crosslingual transfer enables correct recall of some low-frequency facts in non-English languages, primarily via high-frequency English counterparts, but the effect is limited and emerges early in pretraining.
Script similarity (e.g., Latin script) plays a more important role than language family in sustained improvements and crosslingual consistency.
The relationship between fact frequency and recall accuracy emerges early in pretraining and strengthens over time.
papers.limitation:
The scale of crosslingual transfer is limited and typically constrained to relation types involving named entities.
Fact frequency approximation may be ambiguous for languages sharing scripts (e.g., English and French), leading to aggregated counts that might not reflect language-specific frequencies.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of recalling multilingual factual knowledge present in their pretraining data. However, most studies evaluate only the final model, leaving the development of factual recall and crosslingual consistency throughout pretraining largely unexplored. In this work, we trace how factual recall and crosslingual consistency evolve during pretraining, focusing on OLMo-7B as a case study. We find that both accuracy and consistency improve over time for most languages. We show that this improvement is primarily driven by the fact frequency in the pretraining corpus: more frequent facts are more likely to be recalled correctly, regardless of language. Yet, some low-frequency facts in non-English languages can still be correctly recalled. Our analysis reveals that these instances largely benefit from crosslingual transfer of their English counterparts -- an effect that emerges predominantly in the early stages of pretraining. We pinpoint two distinct pathways through which multilingual factual knowledge acquisition occurs: (1) frequency-driven learning, which is dominant and language-agnostic, and (2) crosslingual transfer, which is limited in scale and typically constrained to relation types involving named entities. We release our code and data to facilitate further research at https://github.com/cisnlp/multilingual-fact-tracing.

papers.title: Probing Cross-Lingual Lexical Knowledge from Multilingual Sentence Encoders
papers.research_question: How to best leverage multilingual sentence encoders to represent sub-sentence lexical items (words and phrases) in cross-lingual lexical tasks, and how much cross-lingual lexical knowledge is stored in their parameters.
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders can be 'rewired' into effective cross-lingual lexical encoders via an inexpensive contrastive learning procedure requiring only a small dictionary, exposing more cross-lingual lexical knowledge than is available when using them off-the-shelf.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that multilingual sentence encoders can be effectively transformed into cross-lingual lexical encoders via contrastive fine-tuning, exposing rich lexical knowledge that is particularly beneficial for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual sentence encoders (LaBSE, XMPNET) store more cross-lingual lexical knowledge than vanilla multilingual language models (mBERT, XLM-R).
Contrastive cross-lingual lexical fine-tuning with a small dictionary (1k-5k pairs) substantially improves performance on lexical tasks like BLI, XLSIM, and XEL.
Interpolating the fine-tuned encoder representations with static cross-lingual word embeddings (CLWEs) yields further performance gains, especially for low-resource language pairs.
The gains from contrastive fine-tuning are particularly large for low-resource language pairs, indicating the stored lexical knowledge is crucial in data-scarce scenarios.
Multilingual sentence encoders are more resilient to training data scarcity than static CLWE methods like VECMAP.
papers.abstract: Pretrained multilingual language models (LMs) can be successfully transformed into multilingual sentence encoders (SEs; e.g., LaBSE, xMPNet) via additional fine-tuning or model distillation with parallel data. However, it remains unclear how to best leverage them to represent sub-sentence lexical items (i.e., words and phrases) in cross-lingual lexical tasks. In this work, we probe SEs for the amount of cross-lingual lexical knowledge stored in their parameters, and compare them against the original multilingual LMs. We also devise a simple yet efficient method for exposing the cross-lingual lexical knowledge by means of additional fine-tuning through inexpensive contrastive learning that requires only a small amount of word translation pairs. Using bilingual lexical induction (BLI), cross-lingual lexical semantic similarity, and cross-lingual entity linking as lexical probing tasks, we report substantial gains on standard benchmarks (e.g., +10 Precision@1 points in BLI). The results indicate that the SEs such as LaBSE can be 'rewired' into effective cross-lingual lexical encoders via the contrastive learning procedure, and that they contain more cross-lingual lexical knowledge than what 'meets the eye' when they are used as off-the-shelf SEs. This way, we also provide an effective tool for harnessing 'covert' multilingual lexical knowledge hidden in multilingual sentence encoders.

papers.title: What does it mean to be language-agnostic? Probing multilingual sentence encoders for typological properties
papers.research_question: How do multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties of languages, and how does this vary with different pretraining strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties, but the encoding differs based on pretraining objectives: models with cross-lingual objectives (LASER, XLM) lose typological information in higher layers and create a shared interlingual space, while models with monolingual objectives (M-BERT, XLM-R) retain typological information in all layers and partition the space into language-specific subspaces.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between universality and language-specific information in multilingual encoders, and pretraining objectives influence how typological information is encoded.
papers.key_findings:
All encoders capture some typological properties (word order, pronouns, negation).
M-BERT and XLM-R outperform LASER and XLM on lexical and morphological properties.
Typological information is localizable in lower layers of LASER and XLM, but spread across all layers in M-BERT and XLM-R.
Cross-lingual training leads to more language-agnostic representations but at the cost of losing language-specific typological information in higher layers.
XLM generalizes to languages unseen during pretraining, capturing their typological properties.
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders have seen much success in cross-lingual model transfer for downstream NLP tasks. Yet, we know relatively little about the properties of individual languages or the general patterns of linguistic variation that they encode. We propose methods for probing sentence representations from state-of-the-art multilingual encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM and XLM-R) with respect to a range of typological properties pertaining to lexical, morphological and syntactic structure. In addition, we investigate how this information is distributed across all layers of the models. Our results show interesting differences in encoding linguistic variation associated with different pretraining strategies.

papers.title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Implicitly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
papers.research_question: What is the working mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) in GPT models? The paper investigates whether ICL can be understood as implicit finetuning, where the attention mechanism performs a form of gradient descent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent, leading to the understanding that in-context learning is a form of implicit finetuning. Inspired by this, the paper designs a momentum-based attention mechanism that improves performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning can be understood as implicit finetuning via a meta-optimization process, and this understanding can inspire model design, as demonstrated by the momentum-based attention.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer attention has a dual form with gradient descent, which explains in-context learning as implicit finetuning.
Empirical comparisons show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning in terms of predictions, attention outputs, attention weights, and attention to training tokens.
Momentum-based attention, designed by analogy with gradient descent with momentum, improves performance on language modeling and in-context learning tasks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Transformer-based models and does not consider other architectures.
The dual form is derived using a relaxed linear attention approximation, and the mechanism of standard attention without approximation may be more complex.
Experiments are limited to models up to 2.7B parameters and only classification tasks, leaving larger models and other task types for future work.
future_direction: Study in-context learning for non-Transformer architectures.
Investigate the mechanism of standard Transformer attention without the linear approximation.
Extend the analysis to larger models and other tasks like open-ended generation.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at \url{https://aka.ms/icl}.

papers.title: BERT is Not an Interlingua and the Bias of Tokenization
papers.research_question: Does multilingual BERT use a common interlingual space for different languages, or does it partition representations based on linguistic relationships?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual BERT partitions representations by language rather than using a shared interlingual space, and subword tokenization biases the model towards linguistic phylogenetic structure.
papers.conclusion: Using CCA on the internal representations of BERT, we find that it is not embedding different languages into a shared space. Rather, at deeper layers, BERT partitions the space to better reflect the linguistic and evolutionary relationships between languages. We also find that subword tokenization provides a strong bias to discover linguistic and evolutionary relationships between languages.
papers.key_findings:
Representations for different languages become less similar in deeper layers of BERT.
Fine-tuning causes representations to diverge further in deeper layers.
Deeper layers undergo more change during fine-tuning compared to earlier layers.
CCA similarity between languages reveals a tree structure that mirrors linguistic phylogenetic trees.
Subword tokenization biases the model towards linguistic relationships more than word or character tokenization.
papers.abstract: Multilingual transfer learning can benefit both high-and low-resource languages, but the source of these improvements is not well understood. Cananical Correlation Analysis (CCA) of the internal representations of a pretrained, multilingual BERT model reveals that the model partitions representations for each language rather than using a common, shared, interlingual space. This effect is magnified at deeper layers, suggesting that the model does not progressively abstract semantic content while disregarding languages. Hierarchical clustering based on the CCA similarity scores between languages reveals a tree structure that mirrors the phylogenetic trees hand-designed by linguists. The subword tokenization employed by BERT provides a stronger bias towards such structure than character-and wordlevel tokenizations. We release a subset of the XNLI dataset translated into an additional 14 languages at https://www.github. com/salesforce/xnli_extension to assist further research into multilingual representations.

papers.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Model Merging for Cross-Lingual Transfer in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can modular approaches, such as model merging, improve cross-lingual transfer of mathematical reasoning capabilities to lower-resource languages in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Modular approaches, particularly model merging via Layer-Swapping, effectively improve cross-lingual transfer for mathematical reasoning in low-resource languages, and full fine-tuning followed by parameter resetting outperforms freezing parameters during training.
papers.conclusion: Imposing modularity through model merging is effective for cross-lingual transfer in low-data scenarios, with Layer-Swapping being particularly successful due to the linearity of task vectors and the benefits of full fine-tuning before selective resetting.
papers.key_findings:
All modular solutions (including Layer-Swapping and simultaneous partition SFT) outperform non-modular baselines in cross-lingual transfer for math.
Layer-Swapping, which merges separately trained experts, outperforms more coordinated multi-task fine-tuning approaches.
Full fine-tuning of all parameters followed by resetting unused parameters (via merging) is more effective than freezing those parameters from the start.
The success of Layer-Swapping is partly due to the linearity of task vectors in transformer layers, allowing seamless composition.
Parameter allocations based on prior interpretability work (e.g., top/bottom layers for language, middle layers for math) are effective for modular training.
papers.limitation: The improvements are small because the experiments start from instruction-tuned models that have already undergone extensive post-training, and the fine-tuning datasets are small.
future_direction: Explore more modular configurations and parameter allocation strategies.
Examine other tasks beyond mathematical reasoning.
Improve interpretability to better localize capabilities in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) still struggle across tasks outside of high-resource languages. In this work, we investigate cross-lingual transfer to lower-resource languages where task-specific post-training data is scarce. Building on prior work, we first validate that the subsets of model parameters that matter most for mathematical reasoning and multilingual capabilities are distinctly non-overlapping. To exploit this implicit separability between task and target language parameterization, we develop and analyze numerous modular frameworks to improve the composition of the two during fine-tuning. These methods generally employ freezing parameters or post hoc model merging to assign math and language improvement to different key parts of the LLM. In the absence of in-language math data, we demonstrate that the modular approaches successfully improve upon baselines across three languages, four models, and two fine-tuning paradigms (full and LoRA). Furthermore, we identify the most consistently successful modular method to be fine-tuning separate language and math experts and model merging via Layer-Swapping, somewhat surprisingly. We offer possible explanations for this result via recent works on the linearity of task vectors. We further explain this by empirically showing that reverting less useful fine-tuning updates after training often outperforms freezing them from the start.

papers.title: Learning attention for historical text normalization by learning to pronounce
papers.research_question: How can encoder-decoder architectures, particularly with multi-task learning using pronunciation as an auxiliary task, improve historical text normalization, and how does multi-task learning relate to attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces encoder-decoder architectures for historical text normalization and shows that multi-task learning with a grapheme-to-phoneme auxiliary task improves performance and learns to focus attention similarly to explicit attention mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The presented encoder-decoder approach is effective for historical spelling normalization, and multi-task learning mitigates data scarcity while inducing attention-like mechanisms, providing insights into how MTL works.
papers.key_findings:
Encoder-decoder architectures outperform existing baselines for historical text normalization.
Beam search, lexical filtering, and attention mechanisms provide cumulative performance gains.
Multi-task learning with pronunciation as an auxiliary task improves performance and makes the explicit attention mechanism largely redundant.
Multi-task learning induces weight changes and saliency patterns similar to those learned by an explicit attention mechanism.
The multi-task and attention models show high agreement in the errors they resolve and introduce.
papers.limitation:
The model only considers word forms in isolation, which is problematic for ambiguous cases and makes the task harder for others.
Tokenization differences between historical and modern text present a challenge not addressed by the current approach.
future_direction: Introducing token context to the model, for example by reranking predictions with a language model.
Exploring segment-based normalization (using character input from token n-grams) to handle context and tokenization differences.
papers.abstract: Automated processing of historical texts often relies on pre-normalization to modern word forms. Training encoder-decoder architectures to solve such problems typically requires a lot of training data, which is not available for the named task. We address this problem by using several novel encoder-decoder architectures, including a multi-task learning (MTL) architecture using a grapheme-to-phoneme dictionary as auxiliary data, pushing the state-of-theart by an absolute 2% increase in performance. We analyze the induced models across 44 different texts from Early New High German. Interestingly, we observe that, as previously conjectured, multi-task learning can learn to focus attention during decoding, in ways remarkably similar to recently proposed attention mechanisms. This, we believe, is an important step toward understanding how MTL works.

papers.title: When Alignment Hurts: Decoupling Representational Spaces in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: Does alignment with a high-resource standard language always benefit related low-resource varieties? The paper challenges this assumption by showing that excessive representational entanglement can hinder generative modeling.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an online variational probing framework for subspace decoupling, providing causal evidence that representational entanglement with a high-resource language hinders generative modeling for low-resource varieties.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that representational entanglement with a high-resource language is a critical and addressable bottleneck for generative modeling in closely-related, low-resource language varieties, and provides a causal intervention method to mitigate it.
papers.key_findings:
Excessive representational entanglement with Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) hinders generative performance for low-resource Arabic dialects.
Better generative performance correlates with greater representational separability from MSA in the model's internal geometry.
The proposed online subspace decoupling intervention improves dialectal generation by up to +4.9 chrF++ on individual dialects and +2.0 on average compared to standard fine-tuning.
The intervention leads to a trade-off, with a measured decrease in standard-language (MSA) generation performance.
The method is effective across 25 Arabic dialects, demonstrating the generalizability of the representational dominance phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
The MADAR dataset is composed of relatively short sentences, which may not fully capture model behaviors on tasks requiring longer-form generation.
