The causal claim is based on intervention experiments within a single language family (Arabic), and generalization to other language families requires further validation.
future_direction: Scalable and Efficient Methods
Inference-Time Interventions
Generalization to Other Languages
papers.abstract: Alignment with high-resource standard languages is often assumed to aid the modeling of related low-resource varieties. We challenge this assumption by demonstrating that excessive representational entanglement with a dominant variety, such as Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) in relation to Arabic dialects, can actively hinder generative modeling. We present the first comprehensive causal study of this phenomenon by analyzing and directly intervening in the internal representation geometry of large language models (LLMs). Our key contribution is an online variational probing framework that continuously estimates the subspace of the standard variety during fine-tuning, enabling projection-based decoupling from this space. While our study uses Arabic as a case due to its unusually rich parallel resources across 25 dialects, the broader motivation is methodological: dialectal MT serves as a controlled proxy for generative tasks where comparable multi-variety corpora are unavailable. Across 25 dialects, our intervention improves generation quality by up to +4.9 chrF++ and +2.0 on average compared to standard fine-tuning, despite a measured tradeoff in standard-language performance. These results provide causal evidence that subspace dominance by high-resource varieties can restrict generative capacity for related varieties. More generally, we unify geometric and information-theoretic probing with subspace-level causal interventions, offering practical tools for improving generative modeling in closely related language families and, more broadly, for controlling representational allocation in multilingual and multi-domain LLMs. Code will be released.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: MPN: Leveraging Multilingual Patch Neuron for Cross-lingual Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we perform cross-lingual model editing to update knowledge in multilingual models so that edits in one language generalize to other languages?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a simple method for cross-lingual model editing by training multilingual patch neurons, which can be easily adapted to existing fine-tuning based editing methods to improve their cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: MPN is an effective method for cross-lingual model editing that enhances cross-lingual generalization while maintaining locality and reliability, requiring minimal changes to existing editing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Existing fine-tuning based editing methods possess a certain degree of cross-lingual editing effect, derived from the inherent cross-lingual transfer ability of the multilingual model.
The proposed MPN method improves cross-lingual editing performance without requiring excessive modifications to the original methodology.
MPN achieves an average improvement of about 9% in CLG on the XFEVER dataset and about 12% on the XNLI dataset compared to baselines.
MPN demonstrates strong cross-lingual generalization and good locality, outperforming monolingual editing baselines.
The method is versatile and can be extended to other fine-tuning based editing methods.
papers.limitation:
The cross-lingual editing method is only applied to classification tasks (XFEVER and XNLI) and not to more complex tasks like question-answering.
The XFEVER dataset is created using machine translation without manual verification, which may affect translation quality.
future_direction: Utilize the Bi-zsRE dataset to assess cross-lingual editing performance on question-answering tasks.
Consider using larger models like GPT-4 to potentially improve translation results for dataset creation.
papers.abstract: Large language models are known for encoding a vast amount of factual knowledge, but they often becomes outdated due to the ever-changing nature of external information. A promising solution to this challenge is the utilization of model editing methods to update the knowledge in an efficient manner. However, the majority of existing model editing techniques are limited to monolingual frameworks, thus failing to address the crucial issue of cross-lingual knowledge synchronization for multilingual models. To tackle this problem, we propose a simple yet effective method that trains multilingual patch neuron to store cross-lingual knowledge. It can be easily adapted to existing approaches to enhance their cross-lingual editing capabilities. To evaluate our method, we conduct experiments using both the XNLI dataset and a self-constructed XFEVER dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves improved performance in cross-lingual editing tasks without requiring excessive modifications to the original methodology, thereby showcasing its user-friendly characteristics. Codes will be released soon.

papers.title: Metaphors in Pre-Trained Language Models: Probing and Generalization Across Datasets and Languages
papers.research_question: Does pre-trained language models encode metaphorical knowledge, and how generalizable is this knowledge across languages and datasets?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-trained language models encode metaphorical knowledge, mostly in their middle layers, and this knowledge is transferable across languages and datasets when annotation is consistent.
papers.conclusion: Metaphorical knowledge exists in PLM representations, mainly in middle layers, and is transferable if annotation is consistent across training and testing data.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs encode metaphorical knowledge in their representations.
Metaphorical knowledge is concentrated in the middle layers of PLMs.
The knowledge is transferable across languages (cross-lingual generalization).
The knowledge is transferable across datasets but with larger gaps when annotations are inconsistent.
RoBERTa and ELECTRA encode metaphorical knowledge better than BERT.
papers.limitation: Due to resource limitations, experiments were conducted only on the base versions of models.
future_direction: Explore more the cross-lingual transfer of metaphors and the impact of cross-cultural similarities.
Apply metaphorical knowledge for text generation.
papers.abstract: Human languages are full of metaphorical expressions. Metaphors help people understand the world by connecting new concepts and domains to more familiar ones. Large pretrained language models (PLMs) are therefore assumed to encode metaphorical knowledge useful for NLP systems. In this paper, we investigate this hypothesis for PLMs, by probing metaphoricity information in their encodings, and by measuring the cross-lingual and crossdataset generalization of this information. We present studies in multiple metaphor detection datasets and in four languages (i.e., English, Spanish, Russian, and Farsi). Our extensive experiments suggest that contextual representations in PLMs do encode metaphorical knowledge, and mostly in their middle layers. The knowledge is transferable between languages and datasets, especially when the annotation is consistent across training and testing sets. Our findings give helpful insights for both cognitive and NLP scientists.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 1, Learning Hierarchical Language Structures
papers.research_question: How do language models perform deep reasoning over hierarchical structures, and can we understand their inner workings using synthetic context-free grammars (CFGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers can learn complex context-free grammars and that their hidden states linearly encode non-terminal information, while attention patterns mimic dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn complex hierarchical structures defined by CFGs, and their internal representations and attention patterns align with dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers (GPT variants) can accurately learn and generate strings from synthetic CFGs that require dynamic programming to parse.
Hidden states of the trained transformers linearly encode non-terminal ancestor information almost perfectly.
Attention patterns in the trained models resemble the information flow of dynamic programming, with boundary-based attention.
Relative and rotary positional embeddings are crucial for learning harder CFGs, outperforming absolute positional embeddings.
Training with perturbed data (10% noise) improves robustness to corrupted prefixes.
papers.limitation: The chosen CFGs are synthetic and may not encompass all CFGs; the results are specific to the designed CFG families.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models are effective but complex, and understanding their inner workings and reasoning mechanisms is a significant challenge. Previous research has primarily explored how these models handle simple tasks like name copying or selection, and we extend this by investigating how these models perform recursive language structure reasoning defined by context-free grammars (CFGs). We introduce a family of synthetic CFGs that produce hierarchical rules, capable of generating lengthy sentences (e.g., hundreds of tokens) that are locally ambiguous and require dynamic programming to parse. Despite this complexity, we demonstrate that generative models like GPT can accurately learn and reason over CFG-defined hierarchies and generate sentences based on it. We explore the model's internals, revealing that its hidden states precisely capture the structure of CFGs, and its attention patterns resemble the information passing in a dynamic programming algorithm. This paper also presents several corollaries, including showing why absolute positional embeddings is inferior to relative and rotary embeddings; uniform attention alone is surprisingly effective (motivating our follow-up work on Canon layers); encoder-only models (e.g., BERT, DeBERTa) struggle with deep structure reasoning on CFGs compared to autoregressive models (e.g., GPT); and injecting structural or syntactic noise into pretraining data markedly improves robustness to corrupted language prompts.

papers.title: Morphosyntactic probing of multilingual BERT models
papers.research_question: To what extent do multilingual masked language models encode morphological information, and where in the context does the disambiguating information reside?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an extensive multilingual morphological probing dataset and demonstrates that multilingual BERT models effectively encode morphological information, with a tendency for left context to be more informative than right context.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual BERT models encode morphological information effectively, and the asymmetry in context reliance (left over right) is a general property of language, with exceptions tied to typological facts.
papers.key_findings:
mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa achieve strong accuracy on 247 morphological probing tasks across 42 languages, outperforming an LSTM baseline.
XLM-RoBERTa's larger vocabulary makes it better suited for multilingual probing than mBERT.
Preceding context (left context) tends to hold more information for morphological prediction than following context (right context), which is surprising given the non-directional nature of Transformers.
Perturbation effects on probing accuracy correlate with language typological groups.
German is an outlier in the analysis, with different Shapley value distributions compared to other languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to 42 languages dominated by Indo-European languages.
papers.abstract: Abstract We introduce an extensive dataset for multilingual probing of morphological information in language models (247 tasks across 42 languages from 10 families), each consisting of a sentence with a target word and a morphological tag as the desired label, derived from the Universal Dependencies treebanks. We find that pre-trained Transformer models (mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa) learn features that attain strong performance across these tasks. We then apply two methods to locate, for each probing task, where the disambiguating information resides in the input. The first is a new perturbation method that “masks” various parts of context; the second is the classical method of Shapley values. The most intriguing finding that emerges is a strong tendency for the preceding context to hold more information relevant to the prediction than the following context.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language when processing non-English prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that multilingual language models like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate representations favoring English before shifting to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests that the abstract 'concept space' in multilingual transformers lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding linguistic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate embeddings in middle layers decode to English versions of the correct next token, even when the input and output are non-English.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space (high entropy, no language), concept space (low entropy, English dominates), and output space (target language dominates).
The concept space is biased towards English, indicating an internal pivot language.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The token energy metric shows that latent embeddings have low energy in middle layers and high energy in later layers when the target language is selected.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the Llama-2 family limits generalizability to other models.
Tasks are simple and provide a highly controlled, toy-like context.
Limited understanding of the structure of the concept space in its original high-dimensional form.
The logit lens only grants approximate access to internal beliefs about output; other information remains hidden.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias changes when decreasing the dominance of English during training, e.g., by using different language mixtures or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks, including more culturally sensitive problems and popular use-cases.
Better understand and map out the concept space in its high-dimensional form.
papers.abstract: We ask whether multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language -- a question of key importance for understanding how language models function and the origins of linguistic bias. Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models represent different linguistic phenomena, and are linguistically similar phenomena represented similarly in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using linguistic minimal pairs to measure linguistic similarity in LLMs, revealing that linguistic similarity is influenced by training data, aligns with fine-grained linguistic categories, weakly correlates with semantic similarity, and shows limited cross-lingual alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides insights into LLMs' internal language processing, bridging neural models and linguistic theory, and offers a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages.
Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Dependent on the quality and scope of existing linguistic minimal pair datasets
Limited to three languages, not representing global linguistic diversity
Only captures a fraction of language's complexity with 150 phenomena
future_direction: Developing more high-quality minimal pairs
Broadening language coverage to include more diverse linguistic families
Increasing the range of phenomena studied
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ChenDelong1999/Linguistic-Similarity

papers.title: On the Linguistic Representational Power of Neural Machine Translation Models
papers.research_question: How do neural machine translation models capture linguistic information (morphology, syntax, semantics) in their representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that neural machine translation models learn non-trivial linguistic information in their representations, with a hierarchical organization: lower layers capture local, low-level properties (morphology) and higher layers capture global, high-level properties (syntax, semantics).
papers.conclusion: Deep NMT models trained in an end-to-end fashion, without direct supervision, learn a substantial amount of linguistic information, and the representations are organized in a hierarchical manner.
papers.key_findings:
Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model.
Lexical semantics and non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model.
Representations learned using characters are more informed about word-morphology compared to those learned using subword units.
Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.
The target language impacts the kind of information learned by the MT system, with translation into morphologically-poorer languages leading to better source-side word representations.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent success of deep neural networks in natural language processing and other spheres of artificial intelligence, their interpretability remains a challenge. We analyze the representations learned by neural machine translation (NMT) models at various levels of granularity and evaluate their quality through relevant extrinsic properties. In particular, we seek answers to the following questions: (i) How accurately is word structure captured within the learned representations, which is an important aspect in translating morphologically rich languages? (ii) Do the representations capture long-range dependencies, and effectively handle syntactically divergent languages? (iii) Do the representations capture lexical semantics? We conduct a thorough investigation along several parameters: (i) Which layers in the architecture capture each of these linguistic phenomena; (ii) How does the choice of translation unit (word, character, or subword unit) impact the linguistic properties captured by the underlying representations? (iii) Do the encoder and decoder learn differently and independently? (iv) Do the representations learned by multilingual NMT models capture the same amount of linguistic information as their bilingual counterparts? Our data-driven, quantitative evaluation illuminates important aspects in NMT models and their ability to capture various linguistic phenomena. We show that deep NMT models trained in an end-to-end fashion, without being provided any direct supervision during the training process, learn a non-trivial amount of linguistic information. Notable findings include the following observations: (i) Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model; (ii) In contrast, lexical semantics or non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model; (iii) Representations learned using characters are more informed about word-morphology compared to those learned using subword units; and (iv) Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.

papers.title: From Neurons to Semantics: Evaluating Cross-Linguistic Alignment Capabilities of Large Language Models via Neurons Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the cross-lingual alignment capabilities of large language models in a semantically grounded way?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuronXA, a neuron state-based method for evaluating cross-lingual alignment in LLMs, which shows strong correlation with downstream task performance and transferability.
papers.conclusion: NeuronXA provides a robust and semantically grounded method for evaluating cross-lingual alignment in LLMs, with strong correlations to downstream performance, and has potential for advancing multilingual model research.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron state-based representation more effectively encodes cross-lingual knowledge and improves semantic retrieval accuracy.
NeuronXA achieves high Pearson correlation with downstream tasks (0.9556) and transferability (0.8514).
Alignment scores are highest in middle layers, lower in bottom and top layers, indicating that middle layers contain shared multilingual neurons.
NAS representation reduces directional asymmetry in retrieval tasks.
NeuronXA is robust and generalizable across different base languages and datasets.
papers.limitation:
NeuronXA requires access to the model's intrinsic representations, so it cannot be directly applied to closed-source models.
NeuronXA cannot encompass all perspectives on model capabilities.
future_direction: Extending NeuronXA to evaluate other model capabilities
Applying NeuronXA to expand models to underrepresented languages
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable multilingual capabilities, however, how to evaluate cross-lingual alignment remains underexplored. Existing alignment benchmarks primarily focus on sentence embeddings, but prior research has shown that neural models tend to induce a non-smooth representation space, which impact of semantic alignment evaluation on low-resource languages. Inspired by neuroscientific findings that similar information activates overlapping neuronal regions, we propose a novel Neuron State-Based Cross-Lingual Alignment (NeuronXA) to assess the cross-lingual a lignment capabilities of LLMs, which offers a more semantically grounded approach to assess cross-lingual alignment. We evaluate NeuronXA on several prominent multilingual LLMs (LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, GLM, and OLMo) across two transfer tasks and three multilingual benchmarks. The results demonstrate that with only 100 parallel sentence pairs, NeuronXA achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.9556 with downstream tasks performance and 0.8514 with transferability. These findings demonstrate NeuronXA's effectiveness in assessing both cross-lingual alignment and transferability, even with a small dataset. This highlights its potential to advance cross-lingual alignment research and to improve the semantic understanding of multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: A Study of Cross-Lingual Ability and Language-specific Information in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: What factors influence the cross-lingual ability of multilingual BERT, and does language-specific information exist in its representations?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies datasize and context window size as crucial factors for cross-lingual transferability in multilingual BERT, and introduces Mean Difference Shift (MDS) to manipulate language-specific information for unsupervised token translation and improved cross-lingual transfer.
papers.conclusion: The cross-lingual ability of m-BERT is learned from longer dependency and requires a massive amount of data; language-specific information can be manipulated via simple shifts to improve cross-lingual transfer, opening a new direction for strengthening cross-lingual ability.
papers.key_findings:
With small pretraining data, BERT does not outperform non-contextualized embeddings in cross-lingual ability; with large data, BERT achieves superior cross-lingual alignment.
Breaking down long dependency (smaller window size) hurts cross-lingual ability when pretraining data is large, but helps when data is small.
Language-specific information exists in m-BERT representations and can be extracted via mean difference vectors.
Applying Mean Difference Shift (MDS) to hidden representations can control the output language of m-BERT, enabling unsupervised token translation.
Using MDS to shift representations improves cross-lingual transfer performance on XNLI for most languages, except those with high subword overlap with English.
papers.limitation:
MDS does not improve performance for languages with high subword overlap with English (e.g., Spanish, French) due to shared subwords having different meanings, indicating the need for a more delicate mechanism.
The quality of unsupervised translation using MDS is not acceptable; only token conversion rate is measured, not fluency or accuracy.
future_direction: Develop a more delicate mechanism for applying language-specific shifts that considers differences among vocabularies.
papers.abstract: Recently, multilingual BERT works remarkably well on cross-lingual transfer tasks, superior to static non-contextualized word embeddings. In this work, we provide an in-depth experimental study to supplement the existing literature of cross-lingual ability. We compare the cross-lingual ability of non-contextualized and contextualized representation model with the same data. We found that datasize and context window size are crucial factors to the transferability. We also observe the language-specific information in multilingual BERT. By manipulating the latent representations, we can control the output languages of multilingual BERT, and achieve unsupervised token translation. We further show that based on the observation, there is a computationally cheap but effective approach to improve the cross-lingual ability of multilingual BERT.

papers.title: Triangulation as an Acceptance Rule for Multilingual Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we validate mechanistic explanations for multilingual models to ensure they are causal and invariant across languages and scripts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces triangulation, an acceptance rule for mechanistic interpretability that requires necessity, sufficiency, and invariance across predicate-preserving environments to filter spurious circuits.
papers.conclusion: Triangulation offers a concrete step toward rigorous, transferable mechanistic explanations by requiring cross-environment consistency, allowing circuits that pass to be interpreted with greater confidence as capturing language-agnostic mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Triangulation provides a falsifiable standard for mechanistic claims that filters spurious circuits passing single-environment tests but failing cross-lingual invariance.
Triangulation can be extended to multimodal settings by holding the image fixed and varying the prompt language.
Triangulation enables separation of circuits into visual, linguistic, and spurious categories based on cross-environment invariance.
The method is grounded in causal abstraction theory and provides an approximate transformation score over interchange interventions.
Triangulation requires explicit cue-only falsifiers to reject mechanisms that rely on surface cues rather than predicate information.
papers.limitation:
Multiple circuits may satisfy triangulation if their effects are redundant; triangulation identifies sufficient mechanisms but does not guarantee uniqueness.
The quality of reference families is decisive, and poor-quality families can mislead by either accepting spurious circuits or rejecting genuine circuits.
Causal interventions at scale are computationally expensive, and prioritization strategies are advisable for practical deployment.
When using LLM judges to verify predicate preservation, circularity risks arise if the judge correlates with the model under study.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models achieve strong aggregate performance yet often behave unpredictably across languages, scripts, and cultures. We argue that mechanistic explanations for such models should satisfy a \emph{causal} standard: claims must survive causal interventions and must \emph{cross-reference} across environments that perturb surface form while preserving meaning. We formalize \emph{reference families} as predicate-preserving variants and introduce \emph{triangulation}, an acceptance rule requiring necessity (ablating the circuit degrades the target behavior), sufficiency (patching activations transfers the behavior), and invariance (both effects remain directionally stable and of sufficient magnitude across the reference family). To supply candidate subgraphs, we adopt automatic circuit discovery and \emph{accept or reject} those candidates by triangulation. We ground triangulation in causal abstraction by casting it as an approximate transformation score over a distribution of interchange interventions, connect it to the pragmatic interpretability agenda, and present a comparative experimental protocol across multiple model families, language pairs, and tasks. Triangulation provides a falsifiable standard for mechanistic claims that filters spurious circuits passing single-environment tests but failing cross-lingual invariance.

papers.title: Successor Heads: Recurring, Interpretable Attention Heads In The Wild
papers.research_question: Do recurring, interpretable attention heads (successor heads) exist in large language models, and how do they work?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces successor heads, a class of attention heads that increment tokens in ordinal sequences, and finds that they use abstract mod-10 features across model architectures and scales.
papers.conclusion: Successor heads are a recurring, interpretable component in LLMs that use compositional mod-10 features for incrementation, providing insights into numeric representations and model internals.
papers.key_findings:
Successor heads exist across models from 31M to 12B parameters and across architectures (GPT-2, Pythia, Llama-2).
Successor heads use compositional numeric representations with mod-10 features.
Vector arithmetic with mod-10 features can steer head behavior.
Successor heads are important for low loss on incrementation tasks in natural language data.
Successor heads exhibit polysemanticity (also perform acronym prediction).
papers.limitation:
Mod-10 features do not fully capture the greater-than bias and fail to steer Days and Letters tasks.
The numeric projection might capture more than just the numeric subspace, affecting successor decoding.
future_direction: Future work on how language models represent numeric concepts.
papers.abstract: In this work we present successor heads: attention heads that increment tokens with a natural ordering, such as numbers, months, and days. For example, successor heads increment 'Monday' into 'Tuesday'. We explain the successor head behavior with an approach rooted in mechanistic interpretability, the field that aims to explain how models complete tasks in human-understandable terms. Existing research in this area has found interpretable language model components in small toy models. However, results in toy models have not yet led to insights that explain the internals of frontier models and little is currently understood about the internal operations of large language models. In this paper, we analyze the behavior of successor heads in large language models (LLMs) and find that they implement abstract representations that are common to different architectures. They form in LLMs with as few as 31 million parameters, and at least as many as 12 billion parameters, such as GPT-2, Pythia, and Llama-2. We find a set of 'mod-10 features' that underlie how successor heads increment in LLMs across different architectures and sizes. We perform vector arithmetic with these features to edit head behavior and provide insights into numeric representations within LLMs. Additionally, we study the behavior of successor heads on natural language data, identifying interpretable polysemanticity in a Pythia successor head.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation space closest to English, regardless of input and output languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs perform semantic reasoning in a representation space biased towards English, even for non-English inputs and outputs, as evidenced by logit lens analysis and more effective steering with English-derived vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic decisions in LLMs are predominantly made in a representation space close to English, while non-lexical words are processed in the prompt language, and this behavior varies across models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs route lexical words through English representation space before translating to the target language, while non-lexical words are not necessarily routed through English.
Steering non-English prompts is more effective using English steering vectors than vectors derived from the target language.
Facts are encoded in similar layers across languages, but models have a propensity to answer in English.
The degree of English-routing varies with model multilingualism and size, with more multilingual models routing less through English.
The latent representation structure allows interpolation between facts expressed in different languages while maintaining correctness, indicating shared semantic representations with language-specific components.
papers.limitation:
Tokenization varies across languages, complicating cross-lingual comparisons.
Models may have language confidence and confusion, affecting analysis.
Interpretability methods like steering depend on prompt steerability and may push activations outside the expected distribution.
Alternative methods like sparse autoencoders were not explored due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing more robust evaluation procedures for interpretability methods.
Exploring alternative methods like sparse autoencoders for cross-lingual analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have multilingual capabilities and can solve tasks across various languages. However, we show that current LLMs make key decisions in a representation space closest to English, regardless of their input and output languages. Exploring the internal representations with a logit lens for sentences in French, German, Dutch, and Mandarin, we show that the LLM first emits representations close to English for semantically-loaded words before translating them into the target language. We further show that activation steering in these LLMs is more effective when the steering vectors are computed in English rather than in the language of the inputs and outputs. This suggests that multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation that is heavily shaped by English in a way that is not transparent to system users.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: It’s not Greek to mBERT: Inducing Word-Level Translations from Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: How much word-level translation information is recoverable by multilingual BERT (mBERT) and how is this information stored?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that multilingual BERT encodes word-level translation information that can be extracted via simple template-based and analogies-based methods without fine-tuning, and identifies a language-identity subspace in its representations.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge needed for word-level translation is implicitly encoded in mBERT and is easy to extract with simple methods without fine-tuning; this information is likely stored non-linearly, though some parts can be recovered linearly via a language-identity subspace.
papers.key_findings:
The template-based method achieves high accuracy in word-level translation without any fine-tuning.
The analogies-based method, which manipulates language-encoding components via vector arithmetic, also performs well, indicating some translation information is linearly recoverable.
mBERT representations can be decomposed into language-encoding and language-neutral components using INLP.
An empirical language-identity subspace can be identified within mBERT representations, where representations are well-separated by language.
Most translation information in mBERT is stored non-linearly, but a portion is linearly accessible.
future_direction: Further investigation of the sources of the template-based method's success.
papers.abstract: Recent works have demonstrated that multilingual BERT (mBERT) learns rich cross-lingual representations, that allow for transfer across languages. We study the word-level translation information embedded in mBERT and present two simple methods that expose remarkable translation capabilities with no finetuning. The results suggest that most of this information is encoded in a non-linear way, while some of it can also be recovered with purely linear tools. As part of our analysis, we test the hypothesis that mBERT learns representations which contain both a languageencoding component and an abstract, crosslingual component, and explicitly identify an empirical language-identity subspace within mBERT representations.

papers.title: Representing the bilingual's two lexicons
papers.research_question: Does the separation of lexical representations in bilinguals arise from functional independence in a single neural network rather than from architecturally separate systems?
papers.core_contribution: A single neural network can acquire and represent two languages functionally independently, with separation driven by language-specific input and inter-language similarity, without requiring architecturally separate systems.
papers.conclusion: The single network model provides a functional account of bilingual lexical representation and acquisition, explaining empirical data without innate architectural assumptions and accounting for similarity and frequency effects.
papers.key_findings:
A single network can store two lexicons even with sequential training, avoiding catastrophic interference when sufficient language-specific information is provided.
Functional independence of lexical representations in a single network depends on inter-language similarity, with more similar words showing less independence.
Within-language frequency effects can be observed in a single network, simulating human data previously taken as evidence for separate lexicons.
The model accounts for bilingual priming data, including effects of word similarity and frequency.
Second language learning in a single network does not require architecturally separate systems and can generalize within languages.
papers.abstract: A review of empirical work suggests that the lexical representations of a bilingual's two languages are independent (Smith, 1991), but may also be sensitive to between language similarity patterns (e.g. Cristoffanini, Kirsner, and Mi lech, 1986). Some researchers hold that infant bilinguals do not initially differentiate between their two languages (e.g. Redlinger &amp; Park, 1980). Yet by the age of two they appear to have acquired separate linguistic systems for each language (Lanza, 1992). This paper explores the hypothesis that the separation of lexical representations in biUnguals is a functional rather than an architectural one. It suggests that the separation may be driven by differences in the structure of the input to a comm o n architectural system. Connectionist simulations are presented modelling the representation of two sets of lexical information. These simulations explore the conditions required to create functionally independent lexical representations in a single neural network. It is shown that a single network may acquire a second language after learning a first (avoiding the traditional problem of catastrophic interference in these networks). Further it is shown that in a single network, the functional independence of representations is dependent on inter-language similarity patterns. The latter finding is difficult to account for in a model that postulates architecturally separate lexical representations.

papers.title: Concept Space Alignment in Multilingual LLMs
papers.research_question: Is there a linear mapping between corresponding concepts in different languages in multilingual LLMs, and how does a learned linear mapping generalize to new concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs exhibit high-quality linear concept alignment across languages, but prompt-based embeddings break some of the implicit alignment and generalize worse, especially for typologically distant languages and physical concepts.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs exhibit high-quality, linear concept alignment across different languages, but the ability of supervised maps to generalize varied across different models, languages, and ways of obtaining embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models exhibit very high-quality linear alignments between corresponding concepts in different languages.
Prompt-based embeddings align less linearly than vanilla word embeddings, indicating that some implicitly learned alignments are broken by prompting.
Generalization works best for languages with similar typology (Indo-European) and for abstract concepts.
Abstract concepts exhibit better alignment than physical concepts, which is explained by their higher frequency in training data.
The degree of isomorphism to English is similar across languages, but induced maps generalize much better across typologically related languages.
papers.limitation:
Only six test languages are included due to small overlap between multilingual WordNets, which is too small to draw universally applicable conclusions.
The study is limited to nouns; it is unclear how linear alignment generalizes to other parts of speech.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) seem to generalize somewhat across languages. We hypothesize this is a result of implicit vector space alignment. Evaluating such alignment, we see that larger models exhibit very high-quality linear alignments between corresponding concepts in different languages. Our experiments show that multilingual LLMs suffer from two familiar weaknesses: generalization works best for languages with similar typology, and for abstract concepts. For some models, e.g., the Llama-2 family of models, prompt-based embeddings align better than word embeddings, but the projections are less linear -- an observation that holds across almost all model families, indicating that some of the implicitly learned alignments are broken somewhat by prompt-based methods.

papers.title: Exploring Representational Disparities Between Multilingual and Bilingual Translation Models
papers.research_question: How does the ambient space utilization of model representations differ between bilingual models and one-to-many models? If space utilization differs, what might be driving these differences?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual decoder representations are consistently less isotropic and occupy fewer dimensions than bilingual decoder representations, largely due to language-specific information occupying representational capacity.
papers.conclusion: There is a consistent reduction in representational capacity in multilingual decoders versus bilingual decoders, attributed to language information occupying a significant portion of the representation space.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual decoder representations are less isotropic than bilingual decoder representations across different data resource levels and language pairs.
Multilingual encoder representations are slightly more isotropic than bilingual encoder representations, but the improvement is smaller than the decoder reduction.
The reduction in multilingual decoder isotropy is driven by language-specific information occupying much of the available representation space.
Isotropy decreases with larger training scale, related to the representation degeneration problem.
In multiparallel data, the decoder isotropy reduction is less pronounced for related languages (e.g., Russian and Ukrainian).
papers.limitation:
Models cover at most 3 language families, while modern multilingual translation models cover many more.
Focus on one-to-many models, but many-to-many models may have different behavior.
Focus on encoder-decoder models, but decoder-only translation models may differ.
Work focuses on characterization, not on improving representational capacity.
future_direction: Analyze models with larger language coverage.
Investigate many-to-many multilingual models.
Study decoder-only translation models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual machine translation has proven immensely useful for both parameter efficiency and overall performance across many language pairs via complete multilingual parameter sharing. However, some language pairs in multilingual models can see worse performance than in bilingual models, especially in the one-to-many translation setting. Motivated by their empirical differences, we examine the geometric differences in representations from bilingual models versus those from one-to-many multilingual models. Specifically, we compute the isotropy of these representations using intrinsic dimensionality and IsoScore, in order to measure how the representations utilize the dimensions in their underlying vector space. Using the same evaluation data in both models, we find that for a given language pair, its multilingual model decoder representations are consistently less isotropic and occupy fewer dimensions than comparable bilingual model decoder representations. Additionally, we show that much of the anisotropy in multilingual decoder representations can be attributed to modeling language-specific information, therefore limiting remaining representational capacity.

papers.title: Contributions of Transformer Attention Heads in Multi- and Cross-lingual Tasks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer-based models on cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, and how can important heads be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that pruning a subset of attention heads in multilingual Transformer models (mBERT and XLM-R) generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and introduces a gradient-based method to rank and identify which heads to prune.
papers.conclusion: Pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer models generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and the gradient-based method effectively identifies heads to prune, offering better model interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning attention heads in mBERT and XLM-R generally has positive effects on model performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF).
A gradient-based method can effectively rank attention heads by importance, and pruning the lowest-ranked heads leads to performance improvements.
The important attention heads for a task are shared across languages, as evidenced by high correlation in head rankings across different languages.
Pruning attention heads is beneficial even when training data in the target language is limited, making models more applicable to resource-poor languages.
In multi-source language settings, pruning attention heads also improves performance, and the gradient-based ranking method can be extended to multiple source languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF) and may not generalize to other cross-lingual tasks.
future_direction: Improving model interpretability in other cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, e.g., XNLI and other passage-level classification tasks.
papers.abstract: Weicheng Ma, Kai Zhang, Renze Lou, Lili Wang, Soroush Vosoughi. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2021.

papers.title: Order-Level Attention Similarity Across Language Models: A Latent Commonality
papers.research_question: Do context aggregation patterns across Language Models (LMs) share commonalities?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals significant similarities in Order-Level Attention (OLA) across different language models (OLAS phenomenon) and shows OLA encodes syntactic knowledge, enabling a training-free cross-LM adapter transfer method (TOA).
papers.conclusion: The work reveals a latent commonality in attention patterns across LMs through Order-Level Attention Similarity (OLAS) and demonstrates its utility for enabling training-free cross-model adapter transfer via the proposed TOA method.
papers.key_findings:
Order-Level Attention (OLA) at the same order across different LMs exhibits significant similarities (OLAS phenomenon).
OLA inherently encodes syntactic knowledge of the input text, as demonstrated by training an auxiliary model to predict syntactic dependencies from OLA.
The Transferable OLA Adapter (TOA) enables training-free cross-LM adapter transfer by using OLA as a unified syntactic feature representation.
Transferring TOA from a source LM to an unseen target LM significantly enhances the target LM's performance on downstream tasks like relation extraction and named entity recognition.
Lower-order OLA (e.g., first-order) exhibits more prominent syntactic features and less attention sink phenomenon compared to higher-order OLA and Attention Rollout.
papers.limitation:
The performance of TOA is lower than full fine-tuning of the target model.
The transferability of TOA depends on the similarity between the source and target LMs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we explore an important yet previously neglected question: Do context aggregation patterns across Language Models (LMs) share commonalities? While some works have investigated context aggregation or attention weights in LMs, they typically focus on individual models or attention heads, lacking a systematic analysis across multiple LMs to explore their commonalities. In contrast, we focus on the commonalities among LMs, which can deepen our understanding of LMs and even facilitate cross-model knowledge transfer. In this work, we introduce the Order-Level Attention (OLA) derived from the order-wise decomposition of Attention Rollout and reveal that the OLA at the same order across LMs exhibits significant similarities. Furthermore, we discover an implicit mapping between OLA and syntactic knowledge. Based on these two findings, we propose the Transferable OLA Adapter (TOA), a training-free cross-LM adapter transfer method. Specifically, we treat the OLA as a unified syntactic feature representation and train an adapter that takes OLA as input. Due to the similarities in OLA across LMs, the adapter generalizes to unseen LMs without requiring any parameter updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TOA's cross-LM generalization effectively enhances the performance of unseen LMs. Code is available at https://github.com/jinglin-liang/OLAS.

papers.title: Probing Multilingual BERT for Genetic and Typological Signals
papers.research_question: What typological signals (phylogenetic, geographic, structural) are captured in the representations of multilingual BERT (mBERT)?
papers.core_contribution: mBERT representations capture phylogenetic and geographic signals between languages, and cross-lingual variability in mBERT correlates with diachronic meaning stability.
papers.conclusion: mBERT representations capture phylogenetic and geographic signals, and cross-lingual variability correlates with diachronic stability, contributing to the interpretability of cross-lingual representations.
papers.key_findings:
mBERT lacks fine-grained cross-lingual semantic understanding but captures typological signals.
Language distances from mBERT representations can be used to infer phylogenetic trees that are close to reference trees.
Phylogenetic similarity is the strongest signal in mBERT representations, followed by geographic similarity, while structural similarity is weak.
The phylogenetic signal is present across all layers of mBERT, with initial-middle and final layers performing best.
Cross-lingual variability in mBERT representations (measured by standard deviation) correlates with diachronic meaning stability.
papers.limitation:
mBERT does not properly capture multilingual semantics, as shown by low bilingual lexicon induction performance.
The conclusions should not be used as support for hypotheses relating semantics and language phylogeny (e.g., Sapir-Whorf).
future_direction: Use inferred similarities to predict transfer behavior in downstream tasks between specific language pairs.
papers.abstract: We probe the layers in multilingual BERT (mBERT) for phylogenetic and geographic language signals across 100 languages and compute language distances based on the mBERT representations. We 1) employ the language distances to infer and evaluate language trees, finding that they are close to the reference family tree in terms of quartet tree distance, 2) perform distance matrix regression analysis, finding that the language distances can be best explained by phylogenetic and worst by structural factors and 3) present a novel measure for measuring diachronic meaning stability (based on cross-lingual representation variability) which correlates significantly with published ranked lists based on linguistic approaches. Our results contribute to the nascent field of typological interpretability of cross-lingual text representations.

papers.title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Hidden Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the final layer always yield the best representation for downstream tasks, or can intermediate layers provide better representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intermediate layers in language models often outperform final layers on downstream tasks, and introduces a unified information-theoretic framework to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that intermediate layers often provide superior representations, challenging the default use of final layers, and provides a framework for understanding representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers across diverse architectures and tasks.
Autoregressive models exhibit a pronounced mid-layer compression valley, while masked or bidirectional models show milder changes.
The effect is domain-general, also observed in autoregressive vision transformers.
Chain-of-thought fine-tuning reshapes mid-layer entropy, preserving latent context for multi-step reasoning.
Intermediate layers strike a balance between information compression and signal preservation.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying causes of intermediate layer compression and do explicit finetuning to control compression.
papers.abstract: From extracting features to generating text, the outputs of large language models (LLMs) typically rely on the final layers, following the conventional wisdom that earlier layers capture only low-level cues. However, our analysis shows that intermediate layers can encode even richer representations, often improving performance on a range of downstream tasks. To explain and quantify these hidden-layer properties, we propose a unified framework of representation quality metrics based on information theory, geometry, and invariance to input perturbations. Our framework highlights how each layer balances information compression and signal preservation, revealing why mid-depth embeddings can exceed the last layer's performance. Through extensive experiments on 32 text-embedding tasks across various architectures (transformers, state-space models) and domains (language, vision), we demonstrate that intermediate layers consistently provide stronger features, challenging the standard view on final-layer embeddings and opening new directions on using mid-layer representations for more robust and accurate representations.

papers.title: Separating Tongue from Thought: Activation Patching Reveals Language-Agnostic Concept Representations in Transformers
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop universal concept representations that are disentangled from specific languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides causal evidence that transformer-based LLMs develop language-agnostic concept representations, as shown by activation patching experiments where averaging concept representations across languages improves translation performance.
papers.conclusion: Transformers use language-agnostic latent representations of concepts when processing word-level translation prompts, as evidenced by improved translation performance when averaging concept representations across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The model processes translation tasks by first resolving output language (layers 0-11), then the concept to be translated (layers 12-31).
Activation patching can independently manipulate language and concept information in the model's forward pass.
Patching with the mean representation of a concept across different languages improves translation performance, supporting language-agnostic representations.
These findings generalize across multiple transformer models of varying size, architecture, and training data.
The model can generate natural language descriptions of mean concept representations via activation patching.
papers.limitation: The study only considered simple concepts and did not investigate language-specific concepts.
future_direction: Improving cross-lingual transfer learning by leveraging shared concept spaces
More fine-grained probing to understand concept specialization to language
Reducing computational costs of multilingual training
papers.abstract: A central question in multilingual language modeling is whether large language models (LLMs) develop a universal concept representation, disentangled from specific languages. In this paper, we address this question by analyzing latent representations (latents) during a word-translation task in transformer-based LLMs. We strategically extract latents from a source translation prompt and insert them into the forward pass on a target translation prompt. By doing so, we find that the output language is encoded in the latent at an earlier layer than the concept to be translated. Building on this insight, we conduct two key experiments. First, we demonstrate that we can change the concept without changing the language and vice versa through activation patching alone. Second, we show that patching with the mean representation of a concept across different languages does not affect the models' ability to translate it, but instead improves it. Finally, we generalize to multi-token generation and demonstrate that the model can generate natural language description of those mean representations. Our results provide evidence for the existence of language-agnostic concept representations within the investigated models.

papers.title: How do languages influence each other? Studying cross-lingual data sharing during LM fine-tuning
papers.research_question: To what extent, and under which conditions, do multilingual language models rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the use of Training Data Attribution (TDA) methods, specifically TracIn, to study cross-lingual sharing at the data level in multilingual language models, finding that models rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning and this reliance increases as fine-tuning progresses.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that languages largely influence one another cross-lingually under various conditions, with cross-lingual sharing increasing during fine-tuning and languages playing both reinforcing and complementary roles.
papers.key_findings:
MLMs rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning and this reliance increases as fine-tuning progresses.
Training samples from other languages can both reinforce and complement the knowledge acquired from data of the test language itself.
The model exhibits different cross-lingual behaviour in zero-shot testing compared to when the test language is seen during fine-tuning.
Even with data imbalances, the model largely benefits from cross-lingual sharing.
For parallel datasets, cross-lingual sharing is high, and for non-parallel datasets, it is still observed but to a lesser extent.
papers.limitation:
Computational expense limited the study to 125 test samples.
The method is restricted to relatively easy classification tasks and not generation or sequence labeling tasks.
The analysis focuses on the fine-tuning stage and does not disentangle pre-training effects.
future_direction: Extending influence function methods to sequence tagging tasks for more fine-grained analysis.
Studying the emergence of cross-lingual abilities during pre-training.
Inspiring future work on studying sharing mechanisms within multi-task and multi-modal models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (MLLMs) are jointly trained on data from many different languages such that representation of individual languages can benefit from other languages' data. Impressive performance on zero-shot cross-lingual transfer shows that these models are capable of exploiting data from other languages. Yet, it remains unclear to what extent, and under which conditions, languages rely on each other's data. In this study, we use TracIn (Pruthi et al., 2020), a training data attribution (TDA) method, to retrieve the most influential training samples seen during multilingual fine-tuning for a particular test language. This allows us to analyse cross-lingual sharing mechanisms of MLLMs from a new perspective. While previous work studied cross-lingual sharing at the level of model parameters, we present the first approach to study cross-lingual sharing at the data level. We find that MLLMs rely on data from multiple languages from the early stages of fine-tuning and that this reliance gradually increases as fine-tuning progresses. We further study how different fine-tuning languages influence model performance on a given test language and find that they can both reinforce and complement the knowledge acquired from data of the test language itself.

papers.title: Lost in Multilinguality: Dissecting Cross-lingual Factual Inconsistency in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the underlying causes of cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models, and how can this inconsistency be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models arises from failures in the language transition phase in the final layers, and proposes a linear shortcut method that bypasses these layers to improve both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Language transition errors are a key cause of cross-lingual inconsistency, and the proposed linear shortcut method effectively mitigates this issue, improving model consistency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual language models encode factual knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, transitioning to language-specific spaces only in the final layers.
Incorrect predictions in the target language often occur due to failures during the language transition, even when the correct answer is present in the concept space.
The proposed linear shortcut method, which bypasses final-layer computations, enhances prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
The concept space in LLaMA2 is English-centric, while BLOOM's concept space is more linguistically diverse.
The knowledge recall process in multilingual models involves three stages: relation processing, object extraction in the latent language, and language-specific adaptation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis assumes English as the pivot language, which may limit applicability to language pairs that do not involve English.
The KLAR dataset covers 17 languages but does not fully capture the diversity of world languages.
The shortcut method relies on linear approximation; non-linear approaches might better capture complex transformations.
The study does not explore downstream applications such as multilingual knowledge localization or editing.
future_direction: Expand the investigation to more languages and additional language models to assess broader applicability.
Develop non-linear shortcut methods to better mitigate language transition errors.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLMs) store factual knowledge across languages but often struggle to provide consistent responses to semantically equivalent prompts in different languages.
